lessons.title: Identifying Word Relationships
lessons.concept: Analogy questions test the relationship between a pair of words and ask you to find another pair with the same relationship. Common relationships include part-whole, tool-user, cause-effect, degree/intensity, and category-member.
lessons.formula: Approach: define relationship in pair A:B as 'A is to B as...' -> apply same relationship to options to find C:D.
lessons.worked_example: Finger : Hand :: Toe : ? A finger is a part of a hand; similarly, a toe is a part of a foot. Answer: Foot.
mistakes: Choosing a pair that is merely related by topic but not by the same relationship
Focusing on surface similarity instead of logical relation

lessons.title: Function, Use, and Category Analogies
lessons.concept: Many analogies are based on function (what something does or is used for), worker-tool, or category (type-of). Identify precisely how the first item relates to the second before evaluating options.
lessons.formula: Examples: Pen : Write (tool-function), Carpenter : Wood (worker-material), Apple : Fruit (member-category).
lessons.worked_example: Knife : Cut :: Pen : ? A knife is used to cut; a pen is used to write. Answer: Write.
mistakes: Confusing function with category (e.g., pen is a stationery item, but relation asked may be function)
Selecting an option that fits only one word of the pair
Ignoring the specific role in the relationship

lessons.title: Degree, Sequence, and Opposite Analogies
lessons.concept: Some analogies involve degree/intensity (warm:hot), sequence/order (seed:plant), or opposites (day:night). The relationship type must be preserved exactly in the correct option pair.
lessons.formula: Check whether the pair shows increase/decrease in degree, progression/sequence, or opposition; mirror that in the answer.
lessons.worked_example: Warm : Hot :: Cool : ? Warm to hot shows increasing degree of heat; cool to cold shows increasing degree of cold. Answer: Cold.
mistakes: Picking an opposite when the relation is degree, or vice versa
Missing intensity direction (mild to strong vs strong to mild)
